examples_note: CS_CORE_V1 has no core-level examples in major-cores.json; examples live per specialization, so they are under `specializations.<code>.examples` with the same shape

scene: Handling memory and several tasks running together inside one computer
Dealing with what happens when communication between servers is slow or some of them stop
Changing how data is represented to cut computation time
evidence: Choosing a data structure in a class assignment and writing down why you chose it
Catching where concurrently running parts of a team project fell out of sync
Timing a capstone project, fixing the slow parts and comparing before and after
Writing code in a lab that manages operating system or hardware resources and checking how it behaves
Testing whether a competition entry holds up as input grows and writing down its limits
Getting a code review in a club and keeping a record of what you fixed

evidence_action.first: Pick one feature you worked on in a systems assignment or capstone, and write a one-page design note on how you yourself decided when and in what order resources are acquired and released.
evidence_action.next: Run it repeatedly with the same input to check the results match, and record the resource use of any mismatched runs and the lock scope you changed in your measurement log.

application.resume: In one paragraph, explain how you decided the order for acquiring and releasing resources in a feature you worked on, how you narrowed down mismatches across repeated runs, and how you then changed the lock scope.
interview: What was your reasoning for setting the lock scope that way?
When results differed across repeated runs, what did you measure first?
Did any of the assumptions in your complexity notes break on real input?

scene: Taking requirements and setting module boundaries and interfaces
Deciding the order in which requests are processed and the response format
Setting pass criteria and deployment procedures
evidence: Agreeing first on the format the UI and server would exchange in a class assignment, then building it
Splitting features into units in a team project and deciding who would take on what
Adding test code to a capstone project and running it after every change
Writing down the deployment steps in a lab, including a way to roll back
Preparing for a competition by walking through another service's screens and turning them into a feature list
Collecting where bugs occurred in a club project and fixing them so the same thing would not happen again

evidence_action.first: Pick one module you worked on in a team project, and record your reasoning for where to draw its boundaries as a decision record and an interface contract.
evidence_action.next: Have another teammate implement it from that contract alone, and log the questions that blocked them and the contract items you changed as a result in the change log.

application.resume: In one paragraph, explain how you decided the boundaries of a module you worked on, how you checked whether others could implement it from the interface contract alone, and which items you changed because of questions that blocked them.
interview: What was your reasoning for splitting the module boundaries that way?
How did you fix the parts of the contract where others got stuck?
Which cases did you decide had to be in the test suite, and why?

scene: Assuming an attack and deciding who can use what, and how far
Setting detection rules and response steps
Showing, with evidence, that a standard is met
evidence: Finding and writing down where login or permissions could be broken in a class assignment
Encrypting the values exchanged in a team project and deciding where to keep the keys
Running simulated attacks on a capstone project and separating what was blocked from what got through
Collecting access logs in a lab and finding what looked different from normal
Solving challenges in a competition or contest and writing up how you solved them
Setting inspection items and pass criteria yourself in a club and checking them one by one

evidence_action.first: Pick one system you worked on in a security lab assignment, and record your reasoning for what to allow for whom as a threat list and a permission design table.
evidence_action.next: Match the inspection results one by one against the items the regulations require, and record any mismatched items and the measures you decided on to block them in the inspection report.

application.resume: In one paragraph, explain how you set the permission scope for a system you worked on, what measures you used to block the mismatched items in the inspection report, and how you then changed the inspection items.
interview: What was your reasoning for allowing that level of permission?
Of the items flagged in the inspection, which did you decide to block first?
Where did you decide to keep the keys, and why that location?

scene: Deciding what to draw first within one frame's time
Measuring on every device and taking the slowest as the reference
Deciding when art and sound files are loaded and unloaded
evidence: Setting the controls and rules in a class assignment and building a playable level
Measuring where the screen stuttered in a team project and cutting how much was drawn
Having people play a capstone build and noting where they got lost
Writing movement or collision handling in a lab and fixing where it went wrong
Changing a level's difficulty in a competition and comparing how many players finished
Releasing a level made in a club, collecting feedback and fixing it

evidence_action.first: Pick one scene you worked on in a game assignment or campus contest, and record in the settings table your reasoning for how the time in one frame is split.
evidence_action.next: Measure frame time across different devices, and record in your measurement log where you decided to cut quality and the line you chose to hold anyway.

application.resume: In one paragraph, explain how you split the frame budget for a scene you worked on, what per-device measurements led you to cut or keep, and what you then changed in the graphics settings table.
interview: What was your reasoning for splitting the frame budget that way?
What did you look at to choose where to cut quality?
How did you find where players got lost, and what did you fix?

scene: Cleaning data so it can be used for analysis
Setting evaluation conditions and comparing performance
Gathering cases a model got wrong and finding the cause
evidence: Collecting data for a class assignment and picking out missing fields and odd values
Running two models on the same data in a team project and comparing the results
Deciding first, in a capstone, what exactly you were predicting and choosing the metric to measure it
Splitting training and test data in a lab and checking whether the model also worked on new data
Gathering the cases that did not fit well in a competition and working out why
Writing down the sources of the data used in a club project and what you changed in it

evidence_action.first: Pick one problem you worked on in a data analysis assignment, and record the criteria you set yourself for how to split the data and what to evaluate with, in analysis code and a short explanatory document.
evidence_action.next: Compare against the simplest baseline method under the same conditions, and record the size of the improvement and what the wrong cases had in common in the evaluation results table.

application.resume: In one paragraph, explain how you set the evaluation criteria and data split for a problem you worked on, how you read the comparison with the baseline, and what you changed in the data preparation procedure after looking at the wrong cases.
interview: What was your reasoning for choosing that evaluation criterion?
How did you confirm it really was better than the baseline?
What did the wrong cases have in common, and how did you confirm it?

SPEC_CS_GLOBAL_IT.name: Global IT
SPEC_CS_GLOBAL_IT.note: Building and running services used in many countries

scene: Deciding where to store the languages, date formats and time zones that differ by country
Setting a reference so users in different time zones see the same moment in time
Defining the rules and the range of values exchanged when connecting an overseas service
artifacts: Requirements list with the languages to support
Date and time zone handling rules
Integration contract for an overseas service
evidence: Deciding in a class assignment which wording and date formats a screen used by people from many countries would follow
Coordinating schedules and dividing work with people in different time zones in a team project
Reading English technical documentation in a capstone and turning it into a task list
Connecting to an overseas service's API in a lab and matching the values exchanged
Checking regulations that differ by country in a competition and deciding the usable scope
Collecting and organizing how dates and times are written in countries with different time zones in a club

evidence_action.first: Pick one feature you worked on in a team project, and record in the requirements list your reasoning for the languages to support and the date and time zone handling rules you set yourself.
evidence_action.next: Compare the screens and stored values for users in different time zones using the same cases, and record any mismatches and the display formats you changed as a result in the date and time zone handling rules.

application.resume: In one paragraph, explain how you decided the languages to support and the time zone handling rules for a feature you worked on, and how you found and fixed mismatches on the screens of users in other time zones.
interview: What was your reasoning for choosing those languages and date formats?
What did you look at to find mismatches for users in other time zones?
How did you resolve ambiguous points in documentation written in English?

복잡도.gloss: How much the time or memory needed grows as the input grows

스키마.gloss: A plan that sets which fields the data is stored in

이관.gloss: Moving data, code or operations over to a new system or to the person taking it over

색인.gloss: A separate list built to make lookups faster

잠금.gloss: A mechanism that stops the same data from being changed by two things at once

렌더링.gloss: Drawing what appears on the screen

맞바꿈.gloss: A choice that gives up one thing to gain another
